opening.spoken: This briefing covers Hanxin Zhang's proof that infinitely many pairs of primes sit at most two hundred and forty apart, what its exact certificate establishes, what Nervous Machine reran, and what still has to be read by a person.

short_version.spoken: On August twenty eighth, 2026, Hanxin Zhang proved that infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes differ by at most two hundred and forty, with the discovery credited to the model GPT 5.6 Sol, improving the published record of two hundred and forty six. The proof has two parts: an analytic argument written in the paper, and an exact finite certificate anyone can rerun. Nervous Machine reran the certificate on its own machine under a rule written first. The quick check and the full reconstruction both passed, and the forty-nine-number list is admissible by our own check. What is open is the analytic argument: it has no formal deduction and no referee report. My read: conditionally supported, with the certificate independently reproduced; not yet settled.

what_happened.spoken: The claim appeared on Zenodo and GitHub on the same day in late August. Nervous Machine wrote down what it would check and what it predicted, fetched the nine files at a pinned commit, ran the certificate inside a virtual machine, checked the tuple with its own code, and recorded every outcome.

cycles.spoken: On August twenty eighth, 2026, Hanxin Zhang deposited a paper on Zenodo proving that infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes differ by at most two hundred and forty, with the discovery credited to the model GPT 5.6 Sol, and published a repository with the finite data and exact-arithmetic programs behind it. The analytic argument is in the paper and is not part of the computer check. Three days later Julia Stadlmann posted an independent proof of the same bound without AI, and on September third OpenAI claimed one hundred and eighty six and Axiom Math two hundred and twelve.

cycles.spoken: On November eighth, under a rule written before any file was fetched, Nervous Machine reran Hanxin Zhang's exact certificate for the two hundred and forty bound. The nine files were fetched at a pinned commit and their sizes matched the public listing; the quick check needs only Python's standard library. Run inside a virtual machine, the quick check finished in a fraction of a second and ended with the expected line, an admissible forty-nine-tuple of diameter two hundred and forty. Nervous Machine's own code confirmed that tuple: forty-nine distinct numbers, spanning two hundred and forty, missing at least one remainder for every prime up to forty-seven. The paper's file matched the hash Zenodo publishes. The full exact reconstruction, which recomputes every stored quantity from the coefficient files without a cache, also passed, in 50:12.34 on twenty cores with the pinned library.

gaps.title: The analytic argument has no formal deduction and no referee report
gaps.spoken: Unlike OpenAI's one hundred and eighty six, there is no Lean development here. The nested distribution theorem, the Buchstab identity, the Siegel-Walfisz lemmas and the reductions are a written proof. The certificate checks the finite part only. Until the paper is refereed or the argument is formalized, the claim is conditionally supported whatever the certificate shows.

background.spoken: Results about how evenly primes are spread among remainders modulo large numbers. Proofs of bounded gaps need these as fuel; the more of the range they cover, the smaller the gap that can be proved.
